meta_description: Process mining that survives audit: join-proof event-log forensics, variant-ranked candidates priced on reconciled data, and a kill-reason ledger that makes the pipeline defensible.

blocks.x: Event-log forensics that turn system footprints into a defensible automation pipeline: conformance-checked, variant-ranked, ROI-screened — with kill reasons logged so the backlog your board funds is the backlog reality earned.
Your systems already recorded the process — mining makes it arguable
blocks.sub: Event logs to priced candidates, with join quality proven before discovery

blocks.x: Process mining is evidence gathering, not workshop theater. The systems already record the truth: timestamps in the ERP, states in the ITSM tool, messages on the bus. We reconstruct the actual process from those logs, measure where time and rework concentrate, and price the automation candidates against the mined baseline rather than a manager's estimate.

The deliverable that matters is a ranked pipeline with kill reasons. Most mined candidates die on data quality, permission reality or volume math — recording why is as valuable as the shortlist, because it stops the same idea being re-proposed every year.
What follows is the mining discipline end to end: failure modes, the reference architecture of a mining pipeline, and the console that keeps the backlog honest between cycles.

Case keys before candidate lists
blocks.sub: Join-quality discipline — the reason our mining output survives procurement and audit

blocks.x: Mining programs produce fiction when the event log joins badly: two systems that number the same case differently produce phantom rework, invented loops and variants that exist only in the join error. We therefore prove join quality before any mining runs — key overlap ratios, case-fragmentation rates and a reconciliation sample against source records, reported in the baseline audit. Only then do discovery models run, and they run as variant discovery, not averages: the queue of candidates is priced per variant, with kill reasons logged for every candidate that dies, so the pipeline is an auditable artifact rather than a workshop poster.

Conformance is the bridge from mining to delivery: the discovered flow is compared to the designed flow, and the delta — workarounds, shadow approvals, rework loops — is the actual automation backlog, ranked by priced economics. The continuous miner keeps the artifact alive: a monthly refresh with versioned models, so post-delivery conformance shows whether the automation moved the metric or merely moved the work. The mining console is built for that argument; process owners argue with it, which is exactly the point.

What if our event logs have inconsistent case IDs?

Join quality is proven before discovery. The join-proof gate reconciles a sampled set against system records, and if the keys cannot be defended, mining says so — instead of producing fiction downstream.
Does mining replace talking to the people who do the work?
No. Mined variants frame the interviews; the priced pipeline merges what the logs show with what operators know. Permission fails — 9 per cycle — are resolved with process owners, not around them.
How do candidates carry ROI numbers we can trust?
Each candidate is priced on reconciled frequency and effort deltas, and the pricing basis is part of the evidence pack — finance can audit the arithmetic before funding.
Is this a one-off workshop or an ongoing capability?
A continuous miner: the model is versioned, refreshed on a calendar and guarded by conformance checks that catch drift. The engagement leaves a repeatable artifact, not slides.
What do we get at handover?
The living model, the refresh calendar, the conformance cadence and the candidate ledger with its kill reasons. Process excellence owns it; we support the first two cycles.
